title: Twenty Years of jQuery: How a Little Library Rewired Web Development
gist: jQuery turns 20: it fixed cross-browser JS chaos and seeded a whole 'less code, do more' framework ethos, but native browser APIs and declarative frameworks have made it a legacy dependency that nonetheless still sits on roughly two-thirds of the web, creating a long-tail security and migration overhang.

insights.claim: jQuery 1.0 shipped as a stable release on 26 August 2006, created by John Resig, under the explicit mission that writing JavaScript should be fun.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Marks a 20-year-old dependency whose install base and cultural footprint investors should treat as durable legacy infrastructure, not a fad.
insights.quote: 20yrs ago TODAY the mythical @jquery launched v1.0.

insights.claim: jQuery's $() syntax collapsed cross-browser DOM manipulation, CSS-style selection, chaining, animation, and Ajax into a few lines of code, ending the era of manually working around browser inconsistencies like IE6.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Explains why jQuery achieved near-universal adoption in the 2006-2012 era: it removed a real, costly engineering tax (cross-browser testing).

insights.claim: jQuery lowered the barrier to entry for front-end development, making JavaScript approachable to designers and back-end developers who found the raw language intimidating, seeding the front-end developer population that later frameworks built on.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A platform/tooling company that expands the addressable developer base early can capture outsized ecosystem lock-in later, as jQuery did.
insights.quote: libraries like jQuery "drastically lower the barrier of entry for developers to build rich web applications."

insights.claim: The jQuery plugin ecosystem created a single unified community for JS developers, and that community infrastructure accelerated the success of subsequent tools and ideas beyond jQuery itself.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Community/ecosystem network effects, not just code quality, are what let a library outlive its technical relevance.
insights.quote: jQuery and its ecosystem of plugins created a single community for JS developers.

themes.theme: Displacement by native APIs and frameworks

insights.claim: Browsers standardized native replacements (querySelectorAll, fetch, classList) that now cover most of what developers used to reach for jQuery to accomplish, directly eroding jQuery's original value proposition.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals that the underlying need jQuery filled has been absorbed into the platform itself — a pattern worth watching for other abstraction-layer libraries (e.g. polyfills, utility-belt frameworks).

insights.claim: Declarative frameworks like React and Angular represent a philosophical break from jQuery's procedural DOM-manipulation style, describing what data belongs where rather than issuing step-by-step imperative instructions.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for evaluating any legacy imperative tool being displaced by a declarative successor across other domains (infra-as-code, config management).
insights.quote: Modern frameworks like React and Angular are far more declarative, saying this data belongs to this part, here's how it looks, now take care of it whenever it changes.

themes.theme: Legacy footprint, security overhang, and persistence

insights.claim: W3Techs data shows jQuery still runs on roughly 66% of all websites and the overwhelming majority of sites using any known JS library, propagated largely through WordPress, Drupal, Bootstrap, and Cypress.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A ~66% web-wide install base tied to major CMS/tooling platforms means jQuery is effectively permanent critical infrastructure — relevant to any company selling web security, migration tooling, or legacy-modernization services.

insights.claim: Old jQuery vulnerabilities persist disproportionately in production codebases precisely because the library is so deeply and quietly embedded, making it a structural security overhang rather than a one-off patching problem.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Creates a durable market for extended-support/security-patching vendors (e.g., HeroDevs) servicing deprecated-but-unremovable front-end dependencies.

insights.claim: A steady stream of 'why I still use jQuery' commentary from sources like Docker's engineering blog indicates that some continued usage is a deliberate, non-grudging technical choice rather than pure legacy inertia.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Counters the assumption that all remaining jQuery usage is pure technical debt — some of it reflects an active preference worth understanding before recommending wholesale migration.
insights.quote: helped make the web, and you, what they are today.
